intro.quote: Deleted is not the same as gone, and private is not the same as encrypted.
intro.sideText: Where your data lives, how to lock it up, how to keep copies safe, and how to make it disappear when you’re done with it.

subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: Two kinds of data: what others hold, and what you keep.

blocks.html:
Your data lives in two places. Out there: profiles that apps, websites and data brokers build about you and sell to advertisers, landlords, employers or anyone who pays. With you: the photos, documents and messages on your phone, laptop, USB sticks and cloud accounts.

This lesson covers both. You’ll shrink what’s collected and remove what’s already out there, then protect what you keep: encrypt it so a lost or seized device reveals nothing, back it up so you can’t lose it, strip the hidden details that identify you before you share it, and destroy it properly when you’re done.

blocks.label: Before you start
blocks.html: Encryption is illegal, or draws suspicion, in a few countries. Check the world map of encryption laws if you’re unsure — and remember the easiest data to protect is data you don’t keep.

subsections.title: Terminology
subsections.summary: The words you will run into.

items.title: Data broker
items.html: A company that collects and sells profiles of people, usually without ever dealing with them directly.

items.title: Metadata
items.html: Data about a file — when and where a photo was taken, which phone took it, who wrote a document. Often more revealing than the content.

items.title: Full-disk encryption
items.html: Scrambles everything on a device until you unlock it. FileVault, BitLocker and phone encryption do this. Protects a device that is switched off.

items.title: Encrypted volume / vault
items.html: A locked folder or file (VeraCrypt, Cryptomator) that holds other files and only opens with a password.

items.title: Secure deletion
items.html: Overwriting a file so it can’t be recovered. Emptying the trash only hides it.

items.title: HDD vs. SSD
items.html: Spinning hard drives can be wiped by overwriting. SSDs, USB sticks and SD cards spread data around (wear levelling), so overwriting isn’t reliable — encrypt them instead.

items.title: GDPR / CCPA
items.html: EU and California privacy laws that give you the right to see and delete data held about you.

items.title: 3-2-1 backup
items.html: Three copies of your data, on two kinds of storage, with one kept somewhere else.

subsections.title: Data About You Out There
subsections.summary: Find it, remove it, and stop new leaks.

blocks.html: Search engines, people-search sites and breach databases make it easy for strangers to find your address, phone number and relatives. Start by seeing what’s visible, then remove it — for free, or with a paid service — and cut down what you hand out in future.

items.desc: Find your data, opt out of data brokers and remove yourself from search results.
Ready-to-send removal requests for brokers, GDPR/CCPA and Google.
Small steps that stop new data being collected, tier by tier.

blocks.label: Ask for a copy
blocks.html: Big companies must give you your data on request: Google Takeout, Apple Data & Privacy, and the “download your data” option in most social networks. It shows what they hold — and is your backup before you delete an account.

subsections.title: Encrypt Your Devices
subsections.summary: Lock everything on a lost or stolen device.

blocks.html: Full-disk encryption means a thief or anyone who seizes your device gets scrambled data, not your files. Most devices can do it with a setting.

items.title: iPhone & iPad
items.text: Encrypted automatically as soon as you set a passcode. Use a long alphanumeric passcode rather than six digits.

items.title: Android
items.text: Android 10 and newer encrypt by default. Check under Settings → Security → Encryption & credentials (names vary by phone), and use a strong screen lock.

items.title: Mac
items.text: System Settings → Privacy & Security → FileVault → Turn On. Keep the recovery key in your password manager, not in iCloud if you want Apple out of the loop.

items.title: Windows
items.text: BitLocker on Windows 10/11 Pro, Enterprise or Education (Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption or BitLocker). Add a start-up PIN for extra protection. Home editions can use VeraCrypt system encryption instead.

items.title: Linux
items.text: Full-disk encryption is chosen during installation (“Encrypt the new installation” / LUKS). On an existing system that means backing up and reinstalling.

blocks.label: Shut down, don’t sleep
blocks.html: Encryption only protects a device that is fully powered off. Before crossing a border, going to a protest or leaving a laptop unattended, shut it down.

subsections.title: Encrypt Drives & Files
subsections.summary: USB drives, external disks and sensitive folders.

blocks.html: External drives get lost and seized more often than laptops. Encrypt the whole drive — macOS Disk Utility (format as “encrypted”), BitLocker To Go on Windows, or VeraCrypt on any computer — or keep sensitive files in an encrypted vault.

items.label: VeraCrypt
items.desc: Encrypts whole drives, partitions or file containers. Can hide a second volume behind a decoy password.

items.label: Cryptomator
items.desc: Encrypts a folder file by file — ideal for anything you keep in a cloud.

items.label: Tails
items.desc: A system that runs from a USB stick, leaves no trace and can keep an encrypted persistent folder.

items.label: Tella
items.desc: Hides and encrypts photos, video and audio — built for documenting abuses.

items.text: Lock (unmount) vaults when you step away, before sleep, and before handing over a device
Eject drives in the system before unplugging them
items.details: Pulling a drive out while it’s open can corrupt files.

items.text: Never open an encrypted vault on a computer you don’t trust
items.details: Malware can record your password as you type it.

items.text: Use a long, unique password and store it in your password manager
items.details: See Passwords. There is no “forgot password” for encryption.

items.text: Buy and repair devices through people you trust
items.details: Have second-hand devices wiped and checked before use.

subsections.title: Back Up & Recover
subsections.summary: Copies you can count on — and what to do after a loss.

blocks.html: Encryption without backups is a gamble: a forgotten password or dead drive means losing everything. Keep three copies, on two kinds of storage, one of them somewhere else — encrypted, and on a schedule.

items.desc: The full walkthrough: Time Machine, File History, phone backups, encrypted backup apps and scheduling.

blocks.html: Encrypt before uploading with Cryptomator, or choose a zero-knowledge service such as Filen, Proton Drive, Tresorit, MEGA or Internxt — see cloud storage alternatives. Self-hosters can run Nextcloud.
Stop using the drive immediately — new files can overwrite what you deleted. Then try PhotoRec (all systems) or Recuva (Windows), or the Digital First Aid Kit’s support page.

subsections.title: Remove Identifying Details
subsections.summary: Metadata, faces and locations in what you share.

blocks.html: A photo can carry the exact GPS location, date and phone model it was taken with; a document can carry your name and edit history. Strip it before sharing — and turn off location for the camera so it’s never added.

items.text: Turn off location for your camera app
items.details: Do it before taking photos — removing location afterwards is harder. Check app location permissions while you’re there.

items.text: Remove metadata before you share
items.details: Use one of the tools below. On iPhone you can also tap Options in the share sheet and turn off Location. Check what’s left with Get Info (Mac) or Properties (Windows).

items.text: Black out, don’t blur
items.details: Pixelation and light blur can be reversed. Cover faces, names and screens with a solid, fully opaque box — on iPhone use a filled shape in Markup, not the highlighter.

items.text: Edit on your device, not in a social app
items.details: Uploading the original to a platform gives it the unedited picture, metadata and all.

items.text: Watch your auto-backup
items.details: The un-redacted original may already be in iCloud or Google Photos — delete it there too.

items.label: ExifCleaner
items.desc: Drag and drop to strip metadata from images, videos and PDFs.

items.label: Scrambled Exif
items.desc: Removes metadata when you share a photo.

items.label: MetaX
items.desc: View, edit and delete photo metadata.

items.label: mat2
items.desc: Removes metadata from many file types, including office documents.

items.label: GIMP
items.desc: Free image editor for redacting photos.

items.label: PutMask
items.desc: Blurs faces in videos automatically.

subsections.title: Delete Files for Good
subsections.summary: Why the trash isn’t enough, and what works.

blocks.html: Emptying the trash only marks the space as free; the file stays readable until something overwrites it. How you really delete depends on the drive.

items.title: SSDs, phones, USB sticks, SD cards
items.html: Overwriting isn’t reliable on flash storage. Encrypt the device (so leftovers are unreadable), then delete or factory-reset it.

items.title: Spinning hard drives (HDD)
items.html: Overwrite with a wiping tool. To wipe a whole drive, boot ShredOS from a USB stick, or connect the drive to another computer and use Eraser.

items.label: BleachBit
items.desc: Clears caches, temporary files and browser leftovers, and can wipe free space.

items.label: Eraser
items.desc: Overwrites files, folders and free space on Windows.

items.label: Extirpater
items.desc: Wipes free space on Android. Don’t run it often — it wears out flash memory.

items.label: ShredOS
items.desc: Bootable USB tool that wipes whole hard drives (not SSDs).

subsections.title: Before You Sell or Give Away a Device
subsections.summary: Make sure the next owner gets nothing.

items.text: Back up what you need
Sign out of every account and remove the device
items.details: Apple Account (turn off Find My), Google account, Microsoft account. Otherwise activation lock or account links follow the device.

items.text: Take out the SIM, SD card and any USB sticks
Make sure encryption is on, then factory reset
items.details: On an encrypted phone or Mac, a reset throws away the key, so leftover data is unreadable.

items.text: Old hard drives you won’t reuse: destroy them physically
items.details: Drill several holes through the platters. Don’t burn, microwave or use acid.

items.text: Reinstalling for yourself? Turn encryption on during setup

subsections.title: Share Files Safely
subsections.summary: Send files without handing them to a big platform.

blocks.html: For anything sensitive, use a tool that encrypts or expires the file. Whatever you use, encrypting the file first (for example in a password-protected VeraCrypt container) means the host only ever stores scrambled data.

items.label: OnionShare
items.desc: Share files straight from your computer over Tor. Nothing is stored on anyone’s server.

items.label: share.riseup.net
items.desc: Encrypted uploads from Riseup that expire after 12 hours.

items.label: Disroot Upload
items.desc: Encrypted file upload with a link that expires.

items.label: Tresorit Send
items.desc: End-to-end encrypted transfers with a password option.

blocks.label: Careful
blocks.html: These are run by unknown operators. Assume anything you upload could be seen, scanned or deleted, encrypt files first, and don’t use them for anything you can’t afford to lose or leak.

items.label: Anonym File
items.desc: anonymous file upload and sharing.

items.label: GoFile
items.desc: free, fast sharing with no account.

items.label: Buzzheavier
items.desc: privacy-focused file sharing.

items.label: Easyupload.io
items.desc: temporary uploads with expiry options.

items.label: DropMeFiles
items.desc: temporary sharing with password protection.

items.label: Uguu
items.desc: temporary uploads that delete themselves.

items.label: NiHao Cloud
items.desc: cloud storage and sharing, aimed at sharing with China.
